patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2] mm: unqueue deferred split folios outside the lruvec lock

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2] mm: unqueue deferred split folios outside the lruvec lock

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel to unqueue deferred split folios from a list outside of the lruvec lock, which is held during critical sections that run with IRQs disabled and are highly contended. The existing callers of folio_unqueue_deferred_split() without holding the lruvec lock serve as precedent for this change. A new function, folio_batch_unqueue_deferred_split(), is introduced to unqueue each batch of zero-refcount folios from the deferred split list after the lruvec lock is released and before mem_cgroup_uncharge_folios(). This modification aims to shorten the critical sections under the lruvec lock and reduce contention. Testing with a microbenchmark shows that this patch reduces runtime costs and contention on the lruvec lock.

[PATCH v3] kernfs: allocate inodes and dentry outside kernfs_rwsem

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses long stalls in kernfs due to allocation of inodes and dentries while holding the kernfs_rwsem lock, which can lead to memory reclaim delays and OOM killer activations. The patch allocates inodes outside the lock and frees them if unused, similar to previous commits for other use cases. This change reduces wait times in various scenarios, including cgroupfs operations, and improves overall system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/3] mm: zswap: use separate compression and decompression requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the compression and decompression requests in the zswap module, allowing them to run independently and reducing contention between high-priority loads and low-priority stores. This is done by introducing new data structures for compression and decompression contexts, which are synchronized internally by the codecs and drivers. The change also reduces memory usage on x86-64 systems without PREEMPT_RT or lock debugging. The patch was proposed based on a similar split for zram and has been reviewed and acknowledged by multiple developers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/3] crypto: acomp - enforce MAX_SYNC_COMP_REQSIZE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enforces the limit MAX_SYNC_COMP_REQSIZE when an acomp tfm is initialized, ensuring that all existing algorithms obey this limit. The change involves modifying the crypto_acomp_init_tfm function to check and enforce the request size limit before initializing the algorithm. This patch addresses a potential issue where the request size exceeds the maximum allowed value.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/3] mm: zswap: use stack requests for synchronous decompression
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the zswap decompression mechanism to use stack requests instead of heap requests for synchronous decompression. This change aims to reduce serialization on the per-CPU decompression mutex, which was causing stalls in high-priority loads due to low-priority loads holding onto the mutex after being preempted. The patch allows synchronous algorithms to use on-stack requests, which eliminates the need for a zswap lock and reduces the load path depth by about 270 bytes on x86-64. Asynchronous algorithms continue to use per-CPU requests and mutexes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series reduces contention on loads in zswap by introducing separate requests, waits, and mutexes for compression and decompression. This is done to prevent high-priority loads from waiting for low-priority stores that are still holding the zswap mutex. The patches also enforce a maximum request size for synchronous Crypto ACOMP transforms and use an on-stack request for synchronous decompression. These changes result in improved performance, with read times decreasing by up to 98% in benchmark tests.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

version_history.subject: [PATCH] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the memcpy() function on x86 CPUs without FSRM (Fast String Replication Mode) but with ERMS (Enhanced REP MOVSB). It selects REP MOVSB for large copies of 512 bytes or more, which can be faster than the original implementation. This change is motivated by benchmarks showing that REP MOVSB outperforms the original code in all tested scenarios at 512 bytes and above. The patch specifically targets CPUs like Cooper Lake, where this optimization can significantly reduce memcpy() execution time.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kiryl Shutsemau noted that the patch site is too large and may cause an unconditional jump on FSRM machines, suggesting moving it into memcpy_orig() instead. He also questioned the choice of 512 bytes as the threshold for using REP MOVSB, pointing out that memmove() uses it from 32 bytes on ERMS.
review_comments.raw_body:
This grows the patch site from 2 bytes to 13. On FSRM the replacement is
empty, and 13 bytes is more than ASM_NOP_MAX, so add_nop() puts an
unconditional jump here, executed on every memcpy() call on FSRM
machines. :/

Maybe it is worth moving the patch site into memcpy_orig()? It already
has a 32-byte check. Which brings me to the other question:

Why 512? memmove() uses REP MOVSB from 32 bytes on ERMS. Can we do the
same here? Then we don't need a new branch at all.

--- a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
+++ b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
@@ -50,6 +50,8 @@
 	cmpq $0x20, %rdx
 	jb .Lhandle_tail
 
+	ALTERNATIVE "", __stringify(movq %rdx, %rcx; rep movsb; RET), X86_FEATURE_ERMS
+
 	/*
 	 * We check whether memory false dependence could occur,
 	 * then jump to corresponding copy mode.
-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author acknowledges a mistake in their previous patch, specifically the introduction of an unconditional jump due to FSRM padding, and thanks the reviewer for catching it.

The author tested a 32-byte cutoff on Cooper Lake and found significant performance regressions, but identified 2K as the optimal size for REP MOVSB to outperform memcpy_orig. They modified their patch to use this new threshold and added a helper function for ERMS CPUs.

The author is addressing a concern about performance regressions when using REP MOVSB for copies below 2048 bytes on ERMS CPUs without FSRM. They explain that the issue was due to the destination save in the FSRM replacement, which caused a regression with REP MOVSB. To fix this, they dispatch ERMS through a separate helper and put the destination save in the FSRM replacement, preserving memcpy_orig()'s instructions and placement.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for the review and catching the FSRM padding jump! You're right,
the 13-byte empty replacement introduces an unconditional jump on every call.

---

I tested the 32-byte cutoff on Cooper Lake, which has ERMS without FSRM.
With warmed, aligned buffers, 32-byte copies took 10.906 ns with the
parent and 23.148 ns with the proposal (+112%). The increases at 64, 128 and
256 bytes were about 66%, 65% and 22%. These regressions reproduced across
five process runs and all four tested entry placements.
 
I found 2K to be the spot where REP MOVSB is better. For the entry, I moved
the destination save into the FSRM alternative:

ALTERNATIVE_2 "jmp memcpy_orig", "jmp memcpy_erms", X86_FEATURE_ERMS, \
              "movq %rdi, %rax", X86_FEATURE_FSRM

The ordinary entry then only needs MOV to RCX, REP MOVSB and RET. This gives
FSRM a destination move plus one two-byte NOP, without a padding jump, and
keeps the entry size and scalar layout. A separate memcpy_erms helper checks
2048 and falls back to memcpy_orig below that size. Returns stay in normal
text.

Below is the current state of my patch. What do you think?

---

From: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
Date: Thu, 1 Oct 2026 14:15:12 -0700
Subject: [PATCH] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

Commit 68674f94ffc9 ("x86: don't use REP_GOOD or ERMS for small
memory copies") stopped selecting REP MOVSB from ERMS alone because it
is not suitable for short copies. Consequently, ordinary out-of-line
__memcpy() calls on CPUs with ERMS but without FSRM such as Cooper Lakes
and Skylakes use memcpy_orig() for every length. Its main loop copies
32 bytes per iteration and can be slower than REP MOVSB for large copies,
as measured below on Cooper Lake.

This matters for btrfs zstd decompression. The btrfs-tree commit
e27a6e4823f3 ("btrfs: zstd: avoid a copy in zstd_decompress_bio()")
removes btrfs' copy from a scratch buffer into the page cache by letting
zstd write there directly. It does not remove the copies inside
streaming zstd. ZSTD_decompressStream() still uses memcpy() to flush
decompressed data from its internal output buffer to the supplied page
(zdss_flush), and to stage compressed input when the next block crosses
an input folio supplied by btrfs (zdss_load). In Meta's fleet profile
of x86 kernels, these two btrfs/zstd call sites accounted for about 34%
of the sampled profile weight attributed to memcpy_orig().

On CPUs without FSRM, select REP MOVSB for copies of 2048 bytes and above
when ERMS is present. Keep memcpy_orig() below 2048 bytes. The later FSRM
alternative continues to select REP MOVSB for all sizes, including when
ERMS is not exposed. Copies below 2048 bytes were showing regression
with REP MOVSB as seen below (medians from five runs):

  bytes          orig    REP MOVSB   increase
     32       10.9 ns      23.1 ns     112.3%
     64       13.9 ns      23.1 ns      66.3%
    128       17.5 ns      28.9 ns      65.2%
    256       26.0 ns      31.7 ns      22.1%

Dispatch ERMS through a separate helper and put the destination save in
the FSRM replacement. This keeps the entry alternative at five bytes and
preserves memcpy_orig()'s instructions and placement. FSRM executes the
destination move and one two-byte NOP before its direct REP MOVSB path.

Userspace replicas of the original and patched entry paths were run on
a turbo-disabled Xeon Platinum 8321HC (Cooper Lake, ERMS without FSRM),
at 1.4 GHz. Results below are median times per call from five process
runs of aligned 4 KiB copies at entry offset zero. The replicas use
plain RET; these are assembly microbenchmark results.

Here "warmed" means repeatedly using both buffers. The other rows flush
every cache line intersecting the source or destination before timing.

                                    orig    patched  reduction
  warmed                        371.6 ns   123.4 ns      66.8%
  source flushed                706.5 ns   400.8 ns      43.3%
  destination flushed           457.7 ns   350.0 ns      23.5%

Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
---
 arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S | 13 +++++++++++--
 1 file changed, 11 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
index 12a23fa7c44c5..6b3e203b6087c 100644
--- a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
+++ b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
@@ -31,9 +31,10 @@
  * which the compiler could/should do much better anyway.
  */
 SYM_TYPED_FUNC_START(__memcpy)
-	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
+	/* The FSRM destination move shares the space used by the ERMS jump. */
+	ALTERNATIVE_2 "jmp memcpy_orig", "jmp memcpy_erms", X86_FEATURE_ERMS, \
+		      "movq %rdi, %rax", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
 
-	movq %rdi, %rax
 	movq %rdx, %rcx
 	rep movsb
 	RET
@@ -171,3 +172,11 @@ SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
 	RET
 SYM_FUNC_END(memcpy_orig)
 
+SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_erms)
+	cmpq $2048, %rdx
+	jb memcpy_orig
+	movq %rdi, %rax
+	movq %rdx, %rcx
+	rep movsb
+	RET
+SYM_FUNC_END(memcpy_erms)
-- 
2.53.0-Meta

review_comments.author: David Laight
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where ERMS is present but FSRM is not, and suggested adding a check for this condition to ensure REP MOVSB is used for large copies.

The reviewer expressed concern about adding a conditional branch to all memcpy() calls, suggesting that long copies should be handled by a different function instead of modifying existing ones. They also emphasized the need for testing on various CPUs, including older Zen processors, due to potential differences in behavior.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, 13 Oct 2026 03:04:42 -0700
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

But pretty much all the memcpy() in the kernel are small.
You are adding a conditional branch to all to of them.

If you have somewhere doing long copies then the code should probably
be calling a different function.

You also need to test on a variety of cpu, especially including older zen.
IIRC some of those don't behave as the cpu features might indicate.

Intel cpu going back to ivy bridge (and maybe sandy bridge) treat 'rep movsb'
and 'rep movsq' exactly the same, the only alignment that ever matter is
64 byte alignment (possibly less on ivy/sandy bridge) of the destination
buffer - the copies run twice as fast if 64 byte aligned.
After the initial overhead (which my tests didn't measure) the bytes/clock
was moderately constant across all buffer sizes.
Amd cpu are different, even zen-5 has a big performance hit if (IIRC)
the page offset of source in less than 128 bytes below that of the
destination (the byte alignment doesn't matter).

I need to redo those measurement having worked out hot to time the
instruction setup costs.

David
